bounded-context.name: Shipping
bounded-context.purpose: Schedules and tracks parcels for paid orders. Subscribes to for "what's been ordered" and to for "ok to ship now." Owns carrier selection and tracking-number assignment.

term.name: `Shipment`
term.definition: A physical parcel handed to a carrier, scoped to one Order. Multi-warehouse orders may split into multiple Shipments — the Order has many Shipments, the Shipment has one Order.
term.identity-rule: Stable by `shipmentId`. Carrier-assigned tracking numbers are metadata, not identity (the same Shipment may be re-labelled if a carrier reroute requires it).

term.name: `scheduleShipment`
term.definition: Selects a carrier, generates a label, and records the resulting Shipment. Called once fires for the Order's Invoice.

seam.name: Orders → Shipping
seam.description: Shipping is Orders' downstream customer for the OrderPlaced event stream and for the Order read API. Orders' team commits to Shipping's needs in roadmap discussions; Shipping doesn't dictate Orders' model, but Orders won't ship a version bump that breaks Shipping without coordinating.
seam.rationale: An open-host-service relationship would mean Orders publishes without coordination and any breakage is on the consumer. The reality is that Shipping is the only consumer with a hard operational SLA — losing the event stream means parcels don't ship, which is more expensive than coordinating release timing.

seam.name: Shipping ↔ Inventory release coordination
seam.description: Shipping commits a Reservation to a real shipment; Inventory converts the Reservation to a stock deduction. Neither side drives the other — the release moment is co-designed (a Shipping label generation must always pair with a stock commit; a stock commit without a label is a bug; both are caught at the joint seam).
seam.rationale: Asymmetric framings here would falsely privilege one team's schedule. The release is a joint operation; partnership names that honestly.
